validated_work_order.understanding:
The lot of eight findings PR #73 left open: six are guards in test/web/pages.test.js that read GREEN on the defect they were written to catch, one is a real layout overflow on .awaiting-list li, and one is a false 'measured and safe' out_of_scope entry. I have read both council documents, the code, and — because this machine has /usr/bin/chromium — I have re-measured the disputed browser figures myself in both states and run thirteen of the mutation matrix on a repaired tree. The diagnosis is right and I confirmed it from the code: .awaiting-list is display: grid (styles.css:455) and .awaiting-list li (styles.css:463) declares no overflow-wrap, so the li is a grid item floored at its content's min-content width, and the free text is the decision_id in the <strong> at pages.js:696. I measured, at 320/375/414 with the viewport set by Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride: BEFORE, documentElement.scrollWidth 1672, li scrollWidth 1629, li right edge 1672, computed overflow-wrap 'normal' on li/strong/span, three page-level offenders. AFTER the one declaration: scrollWidth === clientWidth at every width, li scrollWidth 221/276/315, 'anywhere' on li/strong/span, zero offenders. The fix is right and it works.

WHAT I FOUND THAT BOTH DOCUMENTS GOT WRONG, and it is the most consequential thing in this order. The proposal's headline 'correction to v2' is false, and I measured it directly. It claims that on this runner headless Chromium reserves no scrollbar at all, that clientWidth equals innerWidth at 320/375/414, that v2's 305/360/399 'describe a different platform', and that /approvals reads zero offenders here. Every one of those is wrong. I measured, on this runner, with the standard viewport method: innerWidth/clientWidth = 320/305, 375/360, 414/399 — exactly v2's figures, the 15px classic scrollbar and all. /approvals at 320 reads scrollWidth 309 against clientWidth 305 with exactly three li.approval-card@309 offenders. The proposal's own after-fix figures are 15px too wide for the same reason: it reports li scrollWidth 236/291/330 where the truth, which I measured, is 221/276/315 — v2's numbers. So the proposal did not correct v2 on this point; it deleted a correct measurement and replaced it with a wrong one, and it removed AC-10's only real finding on /approvals. The invariant v2 chose — scrollWidth === clientWidth, no platform literals — is right and survives untouched. The literals, and the claim that the /approvals overflow is a platform artefact, do not.

The second thing the critique caught and I confirmed by running it: the proposal's min-width evidence is wrong. The min-width pin lives inside the one test that is red today for the unrelated approval-card matcher, so '71 pass / 1 fail' is unattributable — a min-width failure and the matcher failure are the same red. With only the matcher repaired (/<li class="approval-card"[\s>]/ gives 72/72/0) I ran the family: 12px GREEN, 96px GREEN, and 1rem, 0, 16CH, 8ch all already RED. The proposal states the opposite for 1rem and 16CH, and contradicts its own tests[] case on 16CH. The sharpest defect is 12px, which the ch-only narrowing buys; 1rem was never green and is not what the narrowing buys. AC-5's count of 'nine of these fourteen are green today' is also wrong: I measured eleven.

The third: the render half as specified pins dec_seed_awaiting_1, which I measured at 19 characters. The defect needs 140. The seeded page is byte-identical before and after the change, so that half exercises nothing about the defect, and the proposal's alternative-rejection for it rests on a premise the order itself falsifies two tests later — pages.test.js:1818 builds a 130-character tenant name in-repo and asserts it untruncated, which is exactly the fixture this needs.

The fourth, and it is a design error rather than a measurement: the conflict check the order adds to all eight migrated pins can never fire on six of them, because those six already collect EVERY rule matching their selector, so exempting the pinned set exempts everything that could match. I read all eight sites to confirm it — 1655, 1663, 1759, 1766, 1803 and 1820 are every-match; only the card pin at 1697 uses rules.find, and the .page-title pin at 1633 is the one being moved to every-match. On those six the every-match assertion already IS the same coverage, so the added call is dead code that looks like coverage. The order rejects an alternative for exactly this failure mode and then adopts it.

I kept the proposal's structure almost entirely. It is a good order: the one-declaration product fix, the three shared helpers, the property-filtered collection that answers the v2 rejection, the exact-selector anchoring, the eight read sites, the deliberately-stated forced-colors loosening, the helper contract test, and the one-line repair of the pre-existing red test. What changed is what the measurements and the reading forced.
validated_work_order.root_cause:
Two defects this ticket owns, plus one pre-existing one it does not.

(1) PRODUCT DEFECT, one declaration. src/web/styles.css scopes `overflow-wrap: anywhere` to four card classes (styles.css:394-399). .awaiting-list is display: grid (styles.css:455-461) and .awaiting-list li (styles.css:463-469) is a grid item that declares no overflow-wrap, so its automatic minimum is the min-content width of its content — the decision_id free text in the <strong> at pages.js:696. Measured by me in headless Chromium against a booted instance carrying a 140-character decision_id: scrollWidth 1672 at 320/375/414, li scrollWidth 1629, right edge 1672, computed overflow-wrap 'normal' on li/strong/span, three page-level offenders. After the one declaration at styles.css:463: scrollWidth 305/360/399, equal to clientWidth at every width, li scrollWidth 221/276/315, 'anywhere' on li/strong/span, zero offenders. A grid item's automatic minimum is the token's min-content width, which is exactly what `anywhere` removes and `break-word` does not — the mechanism the stylesheet's own comment at 385-393 exists to defeat.

(2) TEST-INFRASTRUCTURE DEFECT, one missing abstraction, in EIGHT places. test/web/pages.test.js reads src/web/styles.css at lines 345, 359, 1633, 1653, 1693, 1757, 1802 and 1819 and builds its own regex for selectors, bodies or declarations at each. I confirmed by mutation, on a tree with only the approval-card matcher repaired, that these go GREEN today with their assertion defeated: `min-width: 16ch` -> `12px`; `min-width: 16ch` -> `96px`; `min-width: 16ch` deleted leaving a comment naming it; `outline: none` deleted from #main:focus leaving a comment; `margin: 0` deleted from .page-title leaving a comment; an appended `.page-title { margin: 4rem }`; an appended `#main:focus { outline: 3px solid red }`; a media-nested `.approval-card { overflow-wrap: normal }`; and, trivially, everything about .awaiting-list li, which no pin names. The card pin at 1697 survives the at-rule case by accident rather than by design. Two mutations the file already catches are named in tests[] so the order does not overclaim: `.table-scroll { overflow-x: visible }` and `#main > * { min-width: auto }`, both because that test collects every match rather than the first.

(3) PRE-EXISTING, different mechanism, diagnosed here and not fixed here, and REAL ON THIS RUNNER. li.approval-card is a grid item of ul.approval-list (styles.css:367-374, display: grid) and its own rule (styles.css:376-383) is display: grid with no min-width, so its automatic minimum is its min-content width; `#main > *` lifts the floor for main's direct children but not for the li inside the list. Measured by me at a 320px viewport: scrollWidth 309 against clientWidth 305, with exactly three li.approval-card@309 offenders. At 375 and 414 the route reads clean. This is a real page-level overflow of 4px, not a platform artefact — the proposal's contrary claim is the measurement error described in understanding.
validated_work_order.approach:
Two files. One declaration in the stylesheet, and one abstraction in the test file that every stylesheet pin in it then uses — so that at the end of this change there is no second CSS parser left in the suite.

A. Add `overflow-wrap: anywhere;` to the EXISTING `.awaiting-list li` rule in src/web/styles.css, in place among its display/gap/border/radius/padding declarations, with one comment in the same voice and for the same reason as the wrap rule at styles.css:385-393: a grid item is floored at its min-content width, the decision_id is free text, `anywhere` rather than `break-word` because break-word creates the break opportunity but leaves intrinsic sizing alone. NOT as a second rule with the same selector — the new pin's conflict check would read the fix as an override of itself.

B. Add three shared helpers near the top of test/web/pages.test.js, beside H1_HOOK and mainOf, and route all eight stylesheet read sites through them, keeping every existing assertion and every existing failure message verbatim. Only the plumbing moves.

  `cssRules(source)` — strip /* */, then walk with a brace stack. A frame whose selector starts with '@' is a BLOCK whose children are rules; any other frame is a rule whose body is declarations. ';' terminates a declaration inside a rule and a prelude inside an at-rule. Nested rules are emitted with their own selector and a `nested: true` flag. At-rule frames are not emitted. Every rule carries a source index. The proposal and the critique independently parsed the shipped stylesheet to the same result — 68 rules in source order, eight nested: the forced-colors `#main:focus`, the `0%` and `100%` @keyframes steps, `.skeleton`, `#journal-drawer`, `.journal-filters .journal-filter-control`, `.kpi-strip` and `#main`. The keyframe steps are harmless because every lookup is an exact selector match, and the comment must say so, because a later reader who meets them cold will reasonably assume they are a bug. A version that appends nested text to the parent body instead of descending into it drops every nested rule and reinstates the at-rule blind spot exactly, while passing every test in the file as written today.

  `declarations(body, prop)` — one property's values from an already comment-stripped body, anchored on a declaration boundary (start of body, or after a ';') rather than a bare substring, with a trailing chunk after the last ';' treated as a declaration. THE REASON FOR THE ANCHORING, corrected: not the one the proposal gave, which is a false non-reason — 'min-width' is not a substring of 'min-height' (min-w against min-h) and every pin in the file searches `min-width`, not `width`. The two reasons that are real, both of which I measured as green today: (a) a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming one reads as ['16ch'], count 1, green — the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin; (b) a comment beside a real declaration is consumed as the declaration. Name the custom-property case as the third thing the boundary buys: a future `--min-width: 16ch` is matched by a bare substring search and not by a boundary-anchored one, in a stylesheet that already declares twenty custom properties in `:root`. The trailing-chunk clause is a STATED LOOSENING, not a repair, and the proposal is right about this after correcting v2: I measured that dropping the trailing semicolon from `.page-title`'s `line-height: 1.25` and from `#main > *`'s `min-width: 0` is RED today, because both regexes require the ';'. Nothing is silently removed; the file shouts. The tolerance is taken because a helper that cannot read a body whose last declaration has no semicolon is not a CSS reader, and tests[] pins both directions.

  `conflictingOverrides(rules, pinned, selectors, prop)` — the card pin's override loop, lifted out of that test's body and corrected. It takes the property as a fourth argument and filters on `declarations(other.body, prop).length > 0` inside, because the card pin's existing /overflow-wrap\s*:/ filter at pages.test.js:1699 is what makes the comment above it true — a rule that cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. Take the property away and you get one of two failures: drop the filter and a narrow-viewport padding tweak on a pinned selector turns the suite red for a declaration that cannot change the property, re-breaking a tolerance #71 added on purpose; or hardcode overflow-wrap inside and the non-wrap pins get a check that can never fire. `pinned` is the rule OR the SET of rules the calling pin has already asserted on, and every one of them is exempt — the new pin's collection is a set, and without the exemption the fix is reported as an override of itself. A conflict is reported for any rule other than the pinned set, at ANY source index, top-level or nested, declaring `prop` on a comma-split selector part equal to a member of `selectors`. Symmetric in source order, because an override authored above the pinned rule wins at narrow viewports exactly as one below does, and the shipped forced-colors carve-out is the one existing case of that shape.

  THE SELECTOR LOOKUP MUST ANCHOR ON THE SELECTOR'S END — compare a comma-split part to the pinned selector with `===`, never `selector.includes(pinnedSelector)`. '.opportunity-roww' and '.tenant-names' both contain their pinned selector as a substring; I confirmed the current `\s*\{` anchors give both pins their rename protection today, and a substring lookup deletes it across eight pins at once, invisibly, because nothing else in the suite catches a rename.

  WHERE THE CONFLICT CHECK IS CALLED — corrected, and this is the design change. The proposal adds the call to all eight migrated pins. I read all eight sites: 1655 (#main > *), 1663 (.table-scroll), 1759 (.approval-actions), 1766 (.approval-actions input), 1803 (.journal-drawer-body) and 1820 (.tenant-name) each already collect EVERY rule matching their selector, and each asserts the property on every one of them. On those six the every-match assertion IS the same coverage a same-selector conflict check would give, and because the helper exempts the pinned set, the pinned set is every rule that could ever match — so the call can never fire. It is dead code that reads as coverage. Call `conflictingOverrides` only where it can fire: the card pin at 1693 (which uses `rules.find`, so its pinned set is one rule) and the new .awaiting-list pin. On the six, state in the test's comment that the every-match loop is the override check for that selector and no separate call is needed, because it is. This also shrinks a diff the order's own risks already flag as surprising for a one-declaration CSS fix. Add one assertion to the contract test that the pinned set is not the whole selector for any pin that claims the check as coverage, so the distinction cannot rot silently.

  TWO PINS THAT ARE NOT MECHANICAL, both found by running the mutation list against the prototype.

  The .page-title pin becomes wrong if it keeps reading the first match: appended `.page-title { margin: 4rem; }` is green under a first-match check, and the page breaks. It asserts EVERY .page-title rule, which is the shape the #main > * and .table-scroll pin in the same test already uses.

  The #main:focus pin needs an exact count, not a conflict check, and the conflict check is genuinely unavailable there: its one later same-selector rule IS the intentional forced-colors carve-out, so any same-selector override check reports it. So the pin asserts exactly one top-level #main:focus rule, which declares `outline: none`, and exactly one nested one, which is the carve-out. An appended third rule is red on the count, and the carve-out does not move the count because it is nested rather than a second top-level rule. An exemption by index, the alternative, re-creates the blind spot the check exists to remove.

  THE FORCED-COLORS PIN IS THE THIRD PLACE THAT NEEDS CARE, and the loosening is accepted on purpose and pinned. The current regex at pages.test.js:360 is /@media\s*\(forced-colors:\s*active\)\s*\{[^@]*?#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/, and its `[^@]*?` means it only finds the carve-out when it is the first thing in the block. The reader finds it wherever it sits, so the rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE. The assertions that carry the meaning are unchanged — the carve-out exists, declares `outline: 2px solid CanvasText`, and comes after the bare #main:focus rule at equal specificity, both selectors being 1,1,0 — and a mutation that puts another nested rule before the carve-out must still pass, so the loosening is a stated behaviour rather than a silent one. The test's comment says the parser's strictness changed, not the assertion. Keep the `length > 0` guard on the nested-rule lookup specifically, so a reader regression that stopped descending into at-rules cannot make this test pass vacuously on a file with no carve-out at all.

  THE NEW .awaiting-list li PIN, which is the answer to the v2 rejection and the one place the order's own reasoning is the whole point. In the house style of #main > * and .tenant-name rather than a whole-body assertion, and in ONE test with its render half. In order: (a) collect every rule whose comma-split selector part equals `.awaiting-list li` AND whose body declares overflow-wrap — `rules.filter((r) => parts(r).includes('.awaiting-list li') && declarations(r.body, 'overflow-wrap').length > 0)`; (b) require the collection to be NON-EMPTY, with a message that says so, so deleting the declaration and leaving a comment is red; (c) require each collected rule's overflow-wrap values to deepEqual ['anywhere']; (d) run `conflictingOverrides(rules, collected, ['.awaiting-list li', '.awaiting-list li strong', '.awaiting-list li span'], 'overflow-wrap')` and require it to report nothing. THE FILTER IS ON THE COLLECTION, NOT ONLY INSIDE THE HELPER, and that is the sentence v2's rejection asked for: the media-nested rule's selector part IS exactly '.awaiting-list li', so an unfiltered collection takes it in and deepEqual([], ['anywhere']) fails, turning the suite red for a padding declaration. (e) the render half, in the same test, WITH ITS OWN FIXTURE: create a decision whose decision_id is 140 unbreakable characters through the decisions repository against `freshRepos()`, alongside the seeded one, and assert that /journal at override 'partial' emits class="awaiting-list" and an <li data-decision-id=...> whose <strong> holds that id whole. The seeded dec_seed_awaiting_1 is 19 characters — I measured it — and the page renders byte-identically with and without the fix on the seed alone, so a render half that leans on the seed exercises nothing about this defect. pages.test.js:1818 builds a 130-character tenant name in exactly this way and asserts it untruncated; that is the house precedent, two tests below the one being added. It does NOT assert 'and nothing else': .journal-drawer-body already carries overflow-wrap alongside four other declarations in one rule, and a whole-body assertion would force the fix into a second rule with the same selector that the conflict check would then read as an override of itself.

  ONE CONTRACT TEST for the three helpers, driven by fixture strings rather than the shipped stylesheet: a comment-only min-width reads as no declarations; an at-rule-nested rule carries its own selector; a later same-selector rule declaring an UNRELATED property (e.g. `padding: var(--space-3)`) is not a conflict; a media-nested overflow-wrap override IS a conflict; an override authored ABOVE the pinned rule IS a conflict; '.opportunity-roww' does not match '.opportunity-row'; a pin that collects a SET exempts every member of it from its own conflict check; and a pin whose pinned set is the whole selector is distinguishable from one whose pinned set is a single rule. The eight-pin migration otherwise has no automated guard on its own plumbing — every proof it works is a mutation a reviewer runs by hand, and the helpers will outlive this ticket. It is about 30 lines, adds one test, and is the one element here a maintainer can drop without touching the fix.

C. Fix the pre-existing red test, because nothing else in this change is verifiable while it is red: AC-3 and AC-5 both read the file's totals, and a red file makes every count in this order ambiguous. The assertion is /<li class="approval-card">/ and the markup is `<li class="approval-card" data-testid="approval-card" data-approval-card ...>` — a qa/selectors.md-stable data-testid was added to the element after the matcher was written, and the matcher anchors on the closing '>'. The fix is /<li class="approval-card"[\s>]/, which I confirmed takes the file to 72/72/0. `\b` does not work and the reason is worth a comment: after the closing quote both the quote and the following space are non-word characters, so there is no boundary there. While in that helper, drop the `approval.requested` raw-event append from pendingApprovalRepos — grep finds exactly two hits in the whole repository, the helper's own docstring and the append — and rewrite the docstring to say what is actually true: the approval cards come from the seed's three SEEDED_PENDING_IDS (apv_seed_budget_1, apv_seed_campaign_1, apv_seed_geography_1, written through the approvals repository at scripts/seed.js:579), not from a raw event. The existing docstring's cited evidence is also wrong: it points at 'the read at src/web/pages.js:924' and that line is experiment-card markup. Do not write 'four pending' anywhere — three pending, four seeded, one lapsed.

I also read all eight stylesheet read sites and found that six of them already collect every matching rule, so the conflict check the order adds to them can never fire, and I read the two bodies whose trailing semicolons the order proposes tolerating and confirmed both are red today. What holds this at 84 rather than higher is that the migration is still unexecuted: the helpers exist as two prototypes that happen to agree, never as the file that will ship, so every pin verdict in this order is a specification plus a prototype result rather than a run, and I could not change that without writing to the repo. validated_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique's verdict was 'flawed' with the root cause confirmed. I agree with the root cause and I reached a different verdict on the plan, because the falsifiable claims run the other way: the critique is right on all nine of its findings as far as I could check them, and the proposal is the document carrying the false claims. I checked rather than assumed, because the two documents contradict each other on facts I could settle in a browser, and because a critic under instruction to find problems manufactures some.

WHAT THE CRITIQUE CHANGED, and I verified each before applying it.

The scrollbar. This is the one that matters most, and the critique is right and the proposal is wrong. The proposal's headline 'correction to v2' claims this runner reserves no scrollbar, that clientWidth equals innerWidth at 320/375/414, that v2's 305/360/399 'describe a different platform', and that /approvals reads zero offenders here. I measured all four claims on this runner with the standard viewport method and every one is false: 320/305, 375/360, 414/399, and /approvals at 320 reads 309 against 305 with exactly three li.approval-card. The consequence is worse than 'a wrong literal'. The proposal's after-fix li figures are 15px wide for the same reason, and more seriously, it rebuilt AC-10 around a claim that /approvals is clean on the runner where it will be verified. The sweep would then have been a criterion that cannot fail on the route that matters, naming three offenders that do not exist on this runner while the three that do exist are declared out of scope as a platform artefact. I kept v2's invariant — scrollWidth === clientWidth, no literals — which was right all along, and dropped the proposal's replacement of the literals along with the platform claim. Note what this does to the two earlier rounds: the second arbiter's 85 rested partly on distrusting the critic's 309-against-305, and the proposal's 90 rested on the same distrust. I measured it. The brief's original figures were right.

AC-2. Upheld and blocking, and I confirmed it with my own computed-style map over the panel subtree: h2=normal, ul.awaiting-list=normal, li/strong/span=anywhere. 'Every element inside the awaiting panel computes anywhere' is false on a correct fix, because overflow-wrap inherits downward only. I restated it to the three descendants the fix actually reaches and kept the offender sweep as the half that makes it non-vacuous, since a page that never rendered the panel satisfies the first clause alone.

The min-width evidence. Upheld, and this is the finding that shows the proposal measured the wrong thing rather than getting it wrong. The min-width pin lives inside the one test that is red today, so the proposal's '71 pass / 1 fail' readings could not distinguish a min-width failure from the matcher failure — it was the baseline, restated. With only the matcher repaired I ran the family: 12px and 96px GREEN, and 1rem, 0, 8ch and 16CH all already RED. The proposal claims 1rem and 16CH are green today and contradicts its own tests[] case on 16CH. Two things follow that I put in the order: AC-5's 'nine of these fourteen are green today' is eleven, which I measured one at a time; and the ch-only narrowing is credited with 12px and 96px, which is what it actually buys, rather than with 1rem, which `>= 12` was already catching.

The render half. Upheld. I measured the seeded decision_id at 19 characters and confirmed the seeded page renders byte-identically with and without the fix, so the render half as specified exercises nothing about the defect. The proposal's reason for leaning on the seed — that it is the fragility every existing render half carries — is falsified by a test the order itself cites as precedent: pages.test.js:1818 builds a 130-character name in-repo and asserts it untruncated. The render half now builds its own 140-character fixture.

The six dead conflict calls. Upheld, and this is the one that changed the design rather than a measurement. I read all eight sites: 1655, 1663, 1759, 1766, 1803 and 1820 each collect every matching rule and assert the property on every one, so the pinned set is every rule that could ever match and the helper's exemption makes the call unfireable. Only the card pin uses `rules.find`. So the order adds a call at eight sites that can fire at two. I took the critique's first option rather than its second: drop the call at those six, say in each test's comment that the every-match loop is that selector's override check, and let the contract test pin the distinction so it cannot rot silently. Dead code that reads as coverage is worse than an absent call with a reason beside it, and this also shrinks a diff the order's own risks call surprising.

The three minors. All three folded in, because each is a case where the order would have shipped a wrong instruction rather than a wrong number. The declarations() anchoring was justified by a claim that is simply false — 'min-width' is not a substring of 'min-height' — and an implementer anchoring on a false reason anchors wrong; the comment now names the measured one, comment blindness, plus the custom-property hazard, which is the live forward risk in a stylesheet with twenty `:root` properties. The 497/508 citation is wrong, which I confirmed by reading both blocks: four cross-selector overrides, none a same-selector padding tweak, none touching the awaiting list. The requirement stands and the citation goes, which matters because the order repeats that citation in AC-6, in approach and in qa_script. And AC-9's verification command returns exit 1 on the wholly unmigrated file, so it cannot tell migrated from not migrated; the count can, and I measured it — 18 total, 14 of them stylesheet reads, 4 markup scans that must survive.

WHAT I REJECTED FROM THE CRITIQUE, with reasons.

I rejected its suggestion to pin `cssRules(stylesheet).length === 68` as a guard against the reader mishandling a future construct. It is a magic number that breaks on every future stylesheet edit for no semantic reason, which is the maintenance trap this file's own comments exist to prevent; it pins neither semantics nor safety, and the `length > 0` guards already make the reader's failure direction safe. I took the same guard the critique's own regression_risks entry relies on and declined the one it added.

I took the critique's finding 4 in its first form and declined its second. It offered 'widen the watched set to .panel strong and the bare descendant forms' or 'state the hole as a rule rather than a list'. Widening is the wrong move — no list is exhaustive, and a longer list implies a safety it does not have, since `.panel > li > strong` and every other shape a future edit might reach are still outside it. I took the rule form, which is honest, and added a qa_script step that actually appends `.panel strong { overflow-wrap: normal }` and re-runs the sweep, so the hole is tested rather than described.

I did not act on the critique's `!important` note. It is right that `deepEqual(['anywhere'])` reads red on a strictly stronger rule, and right that this is a false red. I left it, because the shipped four-class rule writes plain `anywhere` so `!important` is not this file's idiom, the pin's message is about the property's value, and loosening it now would weaken the exact criterion the previous rejection was about. It is in residual_risks as a known conservative-in-the-safe-direction false red rather than accommodated.

I did not act on its request for a width-by-fixture-length sweep, which is a 'measure more' request rather than a defect. I put the honest version of it in unknown: the order's 140-character fixture is chosen to be safely past the crossing point rather than tuned to it, so the pin's margin is unmeasured.

WHERE I DIFFER FROM BOTH, which is one thing and it is the same thing twice. The proposal is confident and wrong about this runner; I am not going to resolve a factual disagreement between two agents by picking the one whose measurement I did not run. So I ran it. On the two claims that decide acceptance criteria, the proposal is wrong and the critique is right, and the brief's own original figures — 305/360/399, li 221/276/315 — are the ones that survive. Both earlier rounds distrusted the critic's browser numbers without re-measuring them, in opposite directions, and both were half right for the wrong reason: the first arbiter was right to refuse the unsatisfiable equality and right about the mechanism, and wrong to let a literal platform claim ride; the proposer was right about the mechanism and about the trailing semicolons, and wrong about the machine it measured on. Neither document ran the matrix on a tree with the broken matcher repaired, which is the one measurement that would have caught the min-width error, and that is the gap I would most want the next round to close by default rather than by luck.
